summary.title: You should be reading academic computer science papers
summary.one_liner: Academic computer science papers explain where programming ideas came from and offer new ways to solve current problems, and the Papers We Love group is a good starting point for reading them.
keywords: a unified theory of garbage collection
how to read a research paper
learning computer science without formal training
tracy kidder soul of a new machine
takeaways: Academic papers show the history and reasoning behind programming features such as objects, garbage collection and the null pointer.
Reading current research can help when your industry has unique problems that have already been studied, as the Stack Overflow quote puts it: someone else has thought about this problem before.
Papers often need a guide: the Papers We Love community publishes talks that give a primer on how to approach a paper.
Useful starting papers named in the article include Dynamo, A Unified Theory of Garbage Collection, Communicating Sequential Processes and Out of the Tar Pit.
Solutions often combine ideas from several papers, as one team did for load balancing at Comcast.
summary.summary: This Stack Overflow Blog article, a re-publication of a 2022 top post, argues that working programmers should read academic computer science papers to understand where programming ideas came from and to find new solutions. It draws on interviews with three Papers We Love organizers, who describe how they started reading foundational work such as Hoare's Communicating Sequential Processes and how papers helped with real-time monitoring and load balancing problems. The piece also recommends a few starting papers and mentions the Papers We Love repository, which is organized by topic and accepts contributions. It is conversational and offers no step-by-step method for reading papers.
